claim: The majority of mutations studied in animal models are designated as recessive based on the absence of visible phenotypes in germline heterozygotes.
source: The majority of mutations studied in animal models are designated as recessive based on the absence of visible phenotypes in germline heterozygotes.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in genetics research, drawing from established scientific knowledge and conventions.

claim: Genetic studies primarily rely on homozygous loss-of-function to determine gene requirements.
source: Accordingly, genetic studies primarily rely on homozygous loss-of-function to determine gene requirements, and a conceptually-related 'two-hit model' remains the central paradigm in cancer genetics.
evidence: This describes standard methodological approaches in genetics research, based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The 'two-hit model' remains the central paradigm in cancer genetics.
source: Accordingly, genetic studies primarily rely on homozygous loss-of-function to determine gene requirements, and a conceptually-related 'two-hit model' remains the central paradigm in cancer genetics.
evidence: This references an established theory in cancer genetics, drawing from scientific knowledge.

claim: The authors generated inducible alleles that mimic human Juvenile polyposis-associated BMPR1A mutations in Drosophila.
source: To study somatic mutation in Drosophila, we generated inducible alleles that mimic human Juvenile polyposis-associated BMPR1A mutations.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken by the authors, supported by the methods and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Four BMPR1A mutations had no phenotype in heterozygous carriers but exhibited clear tissue-level effects when present in somatic clones of heterozygous cells.
source: Unexpectedly, four of these mutations had no phenotype in heterozygous carriers but exhibited clear tissue-level effects when present in somatic clones of heterozygous cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The studied alleles are recessive when present in the germline but deleterious when present in heterozygous clones.
source: We conclude that these alleles are indeed recessive when present in the germline, but nevertheless deleterious when present in heterozygous clones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Deleterious heteromosaicism represents a 'one-hit' mechanism for disease initiation.
source: This unforeseen effect, deleterious heteromosaicism, suggests a 'one-hit' mechanism for disease initiation that may explain some instances of pathogenesis associated with spontaneous mutation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings, with speculative implications for disease mechanisms.

claim: DNA replication error is estimated to induce mutations at a frequency of 10−9 per replicative cycle.
source: In humans, DNA replication error is estimated to induce mutations at a frequency of 10−9 per replicative cycle such that newborns already exhibit substantial somatic mosaicism at birth (Lynch, 2010; Frank, 2014; Campbell et al., 2015; Fernández et al., 2016; Forsberg et al., 2017; Machiela and Chanock, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Newborns already exhibit substantial somatic mosaicism at birth.
source: In humans, DNA replication error is estimated to induce mutations at a frequency of 10−9 per replicative cycle such that newborns already exhibit substantial somatic mosaicism at birth (Lynch, 2010; Frank, 2014; Campbell et al., 2015; Fernández et al., 2016; Forsberg et al., 2017; Machiela and Chanock, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Additional somatic mutations accumulate over time, resulting in age-dependent incidence of various pathologies.
source: Additional somatic mutations accumulate over time, resulting in the age-dependent incidence of various pathologies, including cancer, X-linked disorders, and neurodevelopmental disease (Veltman and Brunner, 2012; Deng et al., 2014; Frank, 2014; Fernández et al., 2016; Machiela and Chanock, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Spontaneous DNA replication error accounts for two-thirds of cancer mutations.
source: Indeed, it is estimated that spontaneous DNA replication error accounts for two-thirds of cancer mutations (Tomasetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Little is known about the underlying cellular mechanisms by which somatic mutations trigger disease.
source: Nevertheless, little is known about the underlying cellular mechanisms by which somatic mutations trigger disease, primarily because of the technical difficulty of inducing specific mutations in endogenous loci during development of model animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The Drosophila Gal4/UAS system provides a highly flexible platform to drive gene expression in vivo.
source: The Drosophila Gal4/UAS system, for example, provides a highly flexible platform to drive gene expression in vivo (Brand and Perrimon, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Even wild-type alleles expressed at non-physiological levels can produce aberrant phenotypes.
source: Indeed, even wild-type alleles expressed at non-physiological levels can produce aberrant phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Rørth, 1996; Grieder et al., 2007; Akiyama et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The authors used CRISPR/Cas9-dependent genome editing to establish a Flippase (FLP) recombination-dependent allele switch system.
source: To more rigorously investigate the effects of disease-associated mutations in vivo, we used CRISPR/Cas9-dependent genome editing to establish a Flippase (FLP) recombination-dependent allele switch system.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The allele switch system permits the inducible conversion of the wild-type tkv locus to a specific mutant allele.
source: Using human disease-associated alleles of the Drosophila Bone Morphogenetic Protein Receptor 1A (BMPR1A) homologue thickveins (tkv) as a model, our approach permits the inducible conversion of the wild-type locus to a specific mutant allele (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental system, supported by figures showing the design.

claim: In Drosophila, signaling through BMPR1A/Tkv is required to control growth and direct cell fates in the developing wing imaginal disc.
source: In Drosophila, signaling through BMPR1A/Tkv is required to control growth and direct cell fates in the developing wing imaginal disc.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Decapentaplegic (DPP) is the primary ligand for BMPR1A/Tkv in Drosophila.
source: The primary ligand, Decapentaplegic (DPP), is expressed in a narrow band of cells at the anterior-posterior compartment boundary, leading to a downstream phospho-Mothers against dpp (p-Mad) activity gradient in the center of the disc that functions to establish presumptive wing vein regions (Figure 1B–D) (Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996; Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014; Akiyama and Gibson, 2015b; Akiyama and Gibson, 2015a).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: DPP is expressed in a narrow band of cells at the anterior-posterior compartment boundary.
source: The primary ligand, Decapentaplegic (DPP), is expressed in a narrow band of cells at the anterior-posterior compartment boundary, leading to a downstream phospho-Mothers against dpp (p-Mad) activity gradient in the center of the disc that functions to establish presumptive wing vein regions (Figure 1B–D) (Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996; Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014; Akiyama and Gibson, 2015b; Akiyama and Gibson, 2015a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and by data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: DPP signaling leads to a downstream p-Mad activity gradient in the center of the wing disc that functions to establish presumptive wing vein regions.
source: The primary ligand, Decapentaplegic (DPP), is expressed in a narrow band of cells at the anterior-posterior compartment boundary, leading to a downstream phospho-Mothers against dpp (p-Mad) activity gradient in the center of the disc that functions to establish presumptive wing vein regions (Figure 1B–D) (Lecuit et al., 1996; Nellen et al., 1996; Affolter and Basler, 2007; Restrepo et al., 2014; Akiyama and Gibson, 2015b; Akiyama and Gibson, 2015a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and by data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: The tkvGFP>>mCherry allele switch produces no adverse effects on development.
source: In control experiments, we detected no adverse effects of tkvGFP>>mCherry (green) conversion to tkv>mCherry (red).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments described in the study.

claim: UAS-tkv overexpression in the wing pouch using nub-Gal4 caused abnormal phenotypes.
source: In fact, while UAS-tkv overexpression in the wing pouch using nub-Gal4 caused abnormal phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), induction of Tkv-mCherry in the nub-Gal4 domain had no detectable effect on development (Figure 1B–G).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Induction of Tkv-mCherry in the nub-Gal4 domain had no detectable effect on development.
source: In fact, while UAS-tkv overexpression in the wing pouch using nub-Gal4 caused abnormal phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), induction of Tkv-mCherry in the nub-Gal4 domain had no detectable effect on development (Figure 1B–G).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-G.

claim: TkvQ199D is a constitutively active form of the receptor.
source: To further validate the allele switch methodology, we generated a transgenic line that permits inducible in-locus expression of TkvQ199D, a constitutively active form of the receptor (Hoodless et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: w; tkvGFP>>Q199D-mCherry/nub-Gal4; UAS-FLP/+ wing discs exhibited ectopic BMP/DPP activity throughout the Nub expression domain.
source: As expected, w; tkvGFP>>Q199D-mCherry/nub-Gal4; UAS-FLP/+ wing discs exhibited ectopic BMP/DPP activity throughout the Nub expression domain, resulting in both wing disc and adult wing abnormalities (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1H-J.

claim: Expression of TkvQ199D resulted in both wing disc and adult wing abnormalities.
source: As expected, w; tkvGFP>>Q199D-mCherry/nub-Gal4; UAS-FLP/+ wing discs exhibited ectopic BMP/DPP activity throughout the Nub expression domain, resulting in both wing disc and adult wing abnormalities (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1H-J.

claim: BMPR1A is known as a causative gene for Juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS).
source: In humans, BMPR1A is known as a causative gene for Juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS), a condition which predisposes patients to the development of gastrointestinal cancer (Figure 2A) (Howe et al., 2001; Sayed et al., 2002; Greenman et al., 2007; Hardwick et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Juvenile polyposis syndrome predisposes patients to the development of gastrointestinal cancer.
source: In humans, BMPR1A is known as a causative gene for Juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS), a condition which predisposes patients to the development of gastrointestinal cancer (Figure 2A) (Howe et al., 2001; Sayed et al., 2002; Greenman et al., 2007; Hardwick et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Several BMPR1A point mutations have been identified in JPS tissue samples.
source: Although several BMPR1A point mutations have been identified in JPS tissue samples, precisely how each lesion influences receptor activity remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: How each BMPR1A lesion influences receptor activity remains unclear.
source: Although several BMPR1A point mutations have been identified in JPS tissue samples, precisely how each lesion influences receptor activity remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The authors generated allele switch transgenic strains for five JPS-linked point mutations at sites conserved in Drosophila Tkv.
source: To investigate this, we generated allele switch transgenic strains for five JPS-linked point mutations at sites that are conserved in Drosophila Tkv (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach, supported by Figure 2A showing the mutations.

claim: The BMPR1AR443C mutation was detected in JPS patients.
source: First, although the BMPR1AR443C mutation was detected in JPS patients (Sayed et al., 2002; Greenman et al., 2007), the corresponding tkv mutation produced no obvious phenotypes in either the hetero- or homozygous condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–H).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The tkvR409C mutation produced no obvious phenotypes in either the hetero- or homozygous condition.
source: First, although the BMPR1AR443C mutation was detected in JPS patients (Sayed et al., 2002; Greenman et al., 2007), the corresponding tkv mutation produced no obvious phenotypes in either the hetero- or homozygous condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–H).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-H.

claim: Heterozygosity for C40Y, C97R and M442T mutations produced normal wings and mild effects on the p-Mad activity gradient.
source: While heterozygosity for C40Y, C97R and M442T mutations produced normal wings and similarly mild effects on the p-Mad activity gradient (Figure 2D–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), wing discs homozygous for these mutations displayed distinct phenotypes (Figure 2I–K; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Wing discs homozygous for C40Y, C97R and M442T mutations displayed distinct phenotypes.
source: While heterozygosity for C40Y, C97R and M442T mutations produced normal wings and similarly mild effects on the p-Mad activity gradient (Figure 2D–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), wing discs homozygous for these mutations displayed distinct phenotypes (Figure 2I–K; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2I-K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: tkvC40Y-mCherry and tkvC97R-mCherry homozygosity resulted in small wing discs with no detectable p-Mad activity.
source: tkvC40Y-mCherry and tkvC97R-mCherry homozygosity resulted in small wing discs with no detectable p-Mad activity, consistent with strong loss-of-function alleles (Figure 2I and J; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2I and J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: tkvC40Y-mCherry and tkvC97R-mCherry are strong loss-of-function alleles.
source: tkvC40Y-mCherry and tkvC97R-mCherry homozygosity resulted in small wing discs with no detectable p-Mad activity, consistent with strong loss-of-function alleles (Figure 2I and J; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic data shown in the figures.

claim: tkvM442T-mCherry homozygous discs were larger and featured a broadened p-Mad activity gradient.
source: In contrast, tkvM442T-mCherry homozygous discs were larger and featured a broadened p-Mad activity gradient (Figure 2K and M; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), perhaps due to reduced receptor binding and increased BMP/DPP ligand availability.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2K and M and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The broadened p-Mad activity gradient in tkvM442T-mCherry homozygous discs may be due to reduced receptor binding and increased BMP/DPP ligand availability.
source: In contrast, tkvM442T-mCherry homozygous discs were larger and featured a broadened p-Mad activity gradient (Figure 2K and M; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), perhaps due to reduced receptor binding and increased BMP/DPP ligand availability.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenotype.

claim: Residual wild-type clones expressing Tkv-GFP exhibited ectopic signaling activity in tkvM442T-mCherry homozygous wing discs.
source: Supporting this model, occasional residual clones expressing wild-type Tkv-GFP exhibited ectopic signaling activity in tkvM442T-mCherry homozygous wing discs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Residual wild-type clones within tkvC97R-mCherry mutant wing discs showed high levels of BMP activity and frequently produced distinctly rounded outgrowths.
source: Similarly, residual wild-type clones within tkvC97R-mCherry mutant wing discs showed high levels of BMP activity and frequently produced distinctly rounded outgrowths (n = 6/8 discs; Figure 2N–Q).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2N-Q.

claim: The tkvC90R-mCherry variant possessed distinct signaling capabilities depending on the wing disc location.
source: In a third and final allele class, we found that the tkvC90R-mCherry variant possessed distinct signaling capabilities depending on the wing disc location.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: tkvC90R-mCherry homozygosity resulted in weaker p-Mad expression in the wing pouch.
source: While tkvC90R-mCherry homozygosity resulted in weaker p-Mad expression in the wing pouch, the same mutation activated BMP signaling in the hinge region in both hetero- and homozygous discs (Figure 2G,L and M; n = 35 and 32 discs, respectively).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2G, L and M.

claim: tkvC90R-mCherry activated BMP signaling in the hinge region in both hetero- and homozygous discs.
source: While tkvC90R-mCherry homozygosity resulted in weaker p-Mad expression in the wing pouch, the same mutation activated BMP signaling in the hinge region in both hetero- and homozygous discs (Figure 2G,L and M; n = 35 and 32 discs, respectively).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2G, L and M.

claim: Germline tkvC97R heterozygotes exhibited little effect on p-Mad expression and developed normal adult wings.
source: Consistent with the results of uniformly-induced tkvC97R heterozygosity during larval development (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), germline tkvC97R heterozygotes exhibited little effect on p-Mad expression and developed normal adult wings (Figure 3A–D and K).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-D and K.

claim: Sporadic tkvC97R heterozygous clones induced at 72 hr AEL showed aberrant p-Mad expression in wing discs and patterning defects in adult wings.
source: Strikingly, however, when we induced sporadic tkvC97R heterozygous clones at 72 hr AEL, experimental animals showed aberrant p-Mad expression in wing discs and patterning defects in adult wings (Figure 3E–K).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3E-K.

claim: Clones of tkvC97R heterozygous cells exhibited strongly reduced BMP/DPP signaling activity.
source: At the cellular level, clones of tkvC97R heterozygous cells exhibited strongly reduced BMP/DPP signaling activity and increased p-Mad levels in adjacent wild-type cells (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: Clones of tkvC97R heterozygous cells caused increased p-Mad levels in adjacent wild-type cells.
source: At the cellular level, clones of tkvC97R heterozygous cells exhibited strongly reduced BMP/DPP signaling activity and increased p-Mad levels in adjacent wild-type cells (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: Longer duration heat shock increased the number of heterozygous cells present in developing discs and rescued the wing vein phenotypes associated with heterozygous mosaicism.
source: Indeed, longer duration heat shock increased the number of heterozygous cells present in developing discs, and rescued the wing vein phenotypes associated with heterozygous mosaicism (Figure 3K).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Deleterious heteromosaic effects derive from the clonal confrontation between heterozygous and wild-type cells.
source: This indicates that deleterious heteromosaic effects derive from the clonal confrontation between heterozygous and wild-type cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing rescue with increased heterozygosity.

claim: Cell autonomous abrogation of BMP signaling typically leads to clone extrusion and apoptosis.
source: Cell autonomous abrogation of BMP signaling typically leads to clone extrusion and apoptosis (Adachi-Yamada and O'Connor, 2002; Gibson and Perrimon, 2005; Shen and Dahmann, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The majority of homozygous tkvC97R clones were eliminated from the wing epithelia.
source: Consistent with these observations, the majority of homozygous tkvC97R clones were eliminated from the wing epithelia (Figure 4A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither clone extrusion nor apoptosis was observed in wing discs carrying tkvC97R heterozygous clones.
source: However, neither form of cell elimination was observed in wing discs carrying tkvC97R heterozygous clones (Figure 3F,G,I and J; Figure 4B; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3F, G, I, J, Figure 4B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: BMP signal reduction in heterozygous cells was adequate to cause deleterious effects but insufficient to trigger cell removal.
source: We infer that BMP signal reduction in heterozygous cells was adequate to cause deleterious effects but insufficient to trigger cell removal.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that heterozygous clones cause phenotypes but are not eliminated.

claim: Heterozygous cell clones for other recessive tkv alleles elicited similar phenotypes to tkvC97R-mCherry.
source: Further, consistent with a general phenomenon not restricted to tkvC97R-mCherry, heterozygous cell clones for other recessive tkv alleles elicited similar phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Clones heterozygous for tkvC90R-mCherry disrupted p-Mad activity in the developing wing blade region but ectopically activated BMP/DPP signaling in the presumptive hinge territory.
source: In agreement with previous results (Figure 2G and L), we also found that clones heterozygous for tkvC90R-mCherry disrupted p-Mad activity in the developing wing blade region but ectopically activated BMP/DPP signaling in the presumptive hinge territory (n = 26/27 discs; Figure 3—figure supplement 3G–L).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G-L.

claim: tkvC97R heterozygous clones influenced BMP/DPP activity in both eye and haltere discs at the level of Mad phosphorylation.
source: Lastly, we also examined for the effects of deleterious heteromosaicism in other tissues. Although tkvC97R heterozygous clones influenced BMP/DPP activity in both eye and haltere discs at the level of Mad phosphorylation, the adult structures developed normally with no obvious defect (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Adult eye and haltere structures developed normally despite tkvC97R heterozygous clones influencing BMP/DPP activity.
source: Lastly, we also examined for the effects of deleterious heteromosaicism in other tissues. Although tkvC97R heterozygous clones influenced BMP/DPP activity in both eye and haltere discs at the level of Mad phosphorylation, the adult structures developed normally with no obvious defect (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is tissue-specific susceptibility to the same recessive mutations in heterozygous cell clones.
source: These findings suggest a tissue-specific susceptibility to the same recessive mutations in heterozygous cell clones.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that different tissues respond differently to the same mutations.

claim: Recent advances in genome-wide association studies report a substantial accumulation of somatic mutations within individuals, resulting in genetic heterogeneity.
source: Recent advances in genome-wide association studies report a substantial accumulation of somatic mutations within individuals, resulting in genetic heterogeneity (Frank, 2014; Campbell et al., 2015; Fernández et al., 2016; Forsberg et al., 2017; Machiela and Chanock, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Mutational load is associated with the initiation and progression of a number of diseases, including cancer and X-linked disorders.
source: This mutational load is associated with the initiation and progression of a number of diseases, including cancer and X-linked disorders (Veltman and Brunner, 2012; Deng et al., 2014; Fernández et al., 2016; Tomasetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Heteromosaic phenotypes likely emerge from local disparities between wild-type and heterozygous cells.
source: Since animals uniformly heterozygous for the same alleles are phenotypically normal, heteromosaic phenotypes likely emerge from local disparities between wild-type and heterozygous cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between uniform heterozygosity and mosaic heterozygosity.

claim: Cellular heterogeneity associated with homozygous mutant clones is known to perturb tissue integrity by causing cyst formation, cell elimination and apoptosis.
source: Cellular heterogeneity associated with homozygous mutant clones is known to perturb tissue integrity by causing cyst formation, cell elimination and apoptosis (Adachi-Yamada and O'Connor, 2002; Gibson and Perrimon, 2005; Shen and Dahmann, 2005; Hogan et al., 2009; Bielmeier et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: tkv deleterious heteromosaic clones showed no evidence of abnormal tissue architecture or cell death.
source: In contrast, tkv deleterious heteromosaic clones showed no evidence of abnormal tissue architecture or cell death (Figures 3 and 4; Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4 and Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: tkv heterozygous cells disrupted normal wing pattern formation but did not strongly influence growth.
source: Thus, although tkv heterozygous cells disrupted normal wing pattern formation, they did not strongly influence growth and appear to escape from homeostatic surveillance mechanisms such as cell competition (Di Gregorio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed phenotypes and lack of cell elimination.

claim: tkv heterozygous cells appear to escape from homeostatic surveillance mechanisms such as cell competition.
source: Thus, although tkv heterozygous cells disrupted normal wing pattern formation, they did not strongly influence growth and appear to escape from homeostatic surveillance mechanisms such as cell competition (Di Gregorio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that heterozygous cells are not eliminated despite causing phenotypes.

claim: The two-hit hypothesis requires that two independent mutations arise in a single tumor suppressor gene.
source: A prevailing model in cancer genetics, the two-hit hypothesis requires that two independent mutations arise in a single tumor suppressor gene (Nordling, 1953; Knudson, 1971).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational literature on the two-hit hypothesis.

claim: Assuming mutagenesis by random DNA replication error, the probability of two independent mutations hitting the same gene within the same cell lineage is relatively low.
source: Assuming mutagenesis by random DNA replication error, the probability of two independent mutations hitting the same gene within the same cell lineage is relatively low.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on probability and established knowledge about mutation rates.

claim: A single somatic mutation in a putative tumor suppressor causes abnormal development by disrupting the homogeneity of BMPR1A-mediated cellular communication at the tissue level.
source: Here, we report that a single somatic mutation in a putative tumor suppressor causes abnormal development by disrupting the homogeneity of BMPR1A-mediated cellular communication at the tissue level (Figures 3 and 4; Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: A number of disease-linked mutations are known in major signaling pathway components.
source: Given that a number of disease-linked mutations are known in major signaling pathway components, we speculate that deleterious heteromosaicism is not limited to the BMP signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: Deleterious heteromosaicism is not limited to the BMP signaling pathway.
source: Given that a number of disease-linked mutations are known in major signaling pathway components, we speculate that deleterious heteromosaicism is not limited to the BMP signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings and broader knowledge.

claim: The allele switch system allows modeling of the occurrence of spontaneous disease mutations in living tissue.
source: For the first time, genome engineering methods make it possible to model the occurrence of spontaneous disease mutations and investigate their biological consequences in living tissue (Figures 3 and 4; Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This describes the capability of the experimental system developed in the study.

claim: The FLP/FRT-mediated allele switch system uses mCherry-tagged Tkv expression specifically induced in the wing pouch.
source: mCherry-tagged Tkv expression was specifically induced in the wing pouch via FLP/FRT-mediated recombination that eliminates tkv-GFP from the locus.
evidence: This describes the technical details of the allele switch system.

claim: Both Tkv-GFP and Tkv-mCherry expressing animals developed normal adult wings.
source: (D, G) Both Tkv-GFP and Tkv-mCherry expressing animals developed normal adult wings.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1.

claim: TkvQ199D-mCherry expression led to ectopic p-Mad activation.
source: TkvQ199D-mCherry (red) expression led to ectopic p-Mad activation (grey, H, I), resulting in wing malformation (J).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1.

claim: TkvQ199D-mCherry expression resulted in wing malformation.
source: TkvQ199D-mCherry (red) expression led to ectopic p-Mad activation (grey, H, I), resulting in wing malformation (J).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1.

claim: tkv overexpression in the wing pouch by nub-Gal4 led to abnormal p-Mad expression.
source: (C, D) tkv overexpression in the wing pouch by nub-Gal4 (nub-Gal4/UAS-tkv) led to abnormal p-Mad expression (C), resulting in wing patterning defects (D).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: tkv overexpression in the wing pouch by nub-Gal4 resulted in wing patterning defects.
source: (C, D) tkv overexpression in the wing pouch by nub-Gal4 (nub-Gal4/UAS-tkv) led to abnormal p-Mad expression (C), resulting in wing patterning defects (D).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: JPS-associated mutations in BMPR1A are conserved in Drosophila Tkv.
source: (A) Human BMPR1A and Drosophila Tkv protein structures. Conserved JPS-associated mutations are indicated.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 2.

claim: tkvC97R-mCherry heteromosaicism disrupted the p-Mad activity gradient and caused wing vein patterning defects.
source: tkvC97R-mCherry heteromosaicism disrupted the p-Mad activity gradient (grey) and caused wing vein patterning defects (H).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 3.

claim: Longer heat shock generated more uniformly heterozygous cell populations and reduced mosaicism, rescuing wing vein phenotypes.
source: (K) Quantification of adult wing phenotypes in tkvC97R-mCherry heterozygous and heteromosaic animals. Longer heat shock generated more uniformly heterozygous cell populations and reduced mosaicism, rescuing wing vein phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 3.

claim: tkvC97R-mCherry homozygous clones were basally eliminated from wing epithelia.
source: (A–D) tkvC97R homozygous mutant clones were basally eliminated from wing epithelia.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell death was not observed in wing discs possessing tkvC97R heteromosaic clones.
source: (A–D) Cell death was not observed in wing discs possessing tkvC97R heteromosaic clones.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: tkvC40Y and tkvM442T heteromosaicism resulted in aberrant p-Mad expression.
source: (A–F) Deleterious mosaic effects of tkvC40Y and tkvM442T. Wing discs from wild-type control (A, B), tkvGFP>>C40Y-mCherry (C, D), and tkv GFP>>M442T-mCherry (E, F) animals. Tkv-GFP and Tkv*-mCherry are depicted by green and red, respectively. tkvC40Y and tkvM442T heteromosaic resulted in aberrant p-Mad expression (grey, C–F).
